solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

passage_check: Historical/scientific claims check out: 1 degree of longitude per ~4 minutes (15 deg/hr); Nov 18, 1883 was a Sunday; General Time Convention (railroads' association) adopted the zones; telegraph time signals coordinated the switch; 'Day of Two Noons' is the period nickname; Standard Time Act 1918. 'Four' zones is right for the US (the GTC plan also had an Intercolonial zone for eastern Canada, which the passage reasonably omits). 'Dozens of different times' is conservative (often cited as 50-100), so acceptable. 'Noon ... at roughly the moment the sun stood highest' glosses local mean vs apparent time, but 'roughly' covers it.

flags: minor: A is a true but narrow detail (paragraph 2) and will pull some students; that is the intended main-idea trap, and B is still clearly better because it covers paragraphs 4-5.
R037-01.notes: The passage builds toward the final paragraph: noon went from a fact about the sky to an agreement. C distorts the motive (safety was only one reason). D contradicts paragraph 4, which says there was no legal authority.

flags: minor: A is the reversal trap for students who misread 'the sun appears to move westward'. Otherwise this is a one-step extension of the stated Boston, New York, Chicago order.
R037-02.notes: Noon comes later the farther west a town is (Chicago came after Boston and New York), so a town west of Chicago reaches noon later.

flags: minor: B and D are weak distractors that almost no one will pick; C contradicts the time period (before 1883).
R037-03.notes: Each clock was correct for some line and none matched the street: an image of the confusion from separate railroad times.

flags: minor: the key is a close paraphrase of 'had to meet and pass at sidings', so the item is close to a lookup. 'At set times' is a small, reasonable inference.
minor: A, B and D have no support in the passage and are easy to eliminate.
R037-04.notes: Opposing trains on one track had to meet at sidings, so a timing mismatch could put them on the same track at the same time.

flags: minor: 'set back to noon' is slightly looser than the passage, which says the clocks were turned back 'several minutes' so that noon came again (in practice many clocks were stopped and restarted on the standard-noon signal). The key is still the only defensible choice.
minor: the key closely paraphrases one sentence of paragraph 3 (lookup); B reverses the direction of the change.
minor: some thematic overlap with R037-08, since both involve clock noon departing from sun noon.
R037-05.notes: In towns east of the zone's central meridian, local noon had already passed; the clocks were turned back, so noon struck again.

flags: minor: A is a strong mirror-image trap (it reverses which part the author grants); the 'qualified X' parallel structure of A and D makes this a careful-reading test, which is fine.
R037-06.notes: 'They were, in a sense, correct: the railroads had no legal authority' (agreement on the law), then 'They had something more effective' (the network, which the objectors overlooked). B overstates, C contradicts 'striking'.

flags: minor: a familiar meaning in context; A and D are weak; B ('attractive') is the only real distractor.
R037-07.notes: 'What is striking is who made the change' means what is notable or remarkable.

flags: minor: A illustrates the old meaning and could catch students who match the 'shadow' wording in the last paragraph; C illustrates the pre-1883 confusion, not the new meaning.
R037-08.notes: Under standard time, noon is a convention and can differ from the sun's highest point. D reverses the change, tying clocks back to the sky.

flags: minor: overlaps with R037-06 and R037-01 choice D (all turn on 'no legal authority, yet adopted'); having read R037-09 makes R037-01 D easier to eliminate, but nothing gives an answer away.
minor: B, C and D have no support in the passage and are easy to eliminate.
R037-09.notes: The 35-year gap shows that adoption happened through practice: the railroads announced it and the public followed long before the law.
